title: Nankana, the full story
hookLine: at Guru Nanak's birthplace in 1921 the mahant's men killed many peaceful reformers, including Bhai Lachhman Singh

lines: AN OLD JAND TREE IN A COURTYARD.
cards: In the courtyard of a gurdwara at Nankana Sahib stands an old jand tree, a thorny tree of the Punjab plains. Pilgrims stop beside it and bow their heads. It isn't there for its shade.
Sikhs remember what was done at that tree on a morning in 1921, at the place tradition holds as Guru Nanak's birthplace. To understand why people bow to a tree, you need the whole story.

teach.h: A SHRINE HELD BY A MAHANT.
teach.b: The gurdwara at Guru Nanak's birthplace was held by a mahant, Narain Das, who ran it as his own.
Reformers accused him of misusing its wealth and allowing wrongs within its walls, and meant to bring it under the Panth's care. Accounts say the mahant knew they were coming and gathered armed men.
A band of reformers led by Bhai Lachhman Singh reached the gurdwara early in the morning.

teach.h: RECITING BEFORE THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.
teach.b: They went in, sat down before the Guru Granth Sahib, and began to recite.

teach.h: THE GATES SHUT, AND THE ATTACK.
teach.b: The gates were shut behind them, and the mahant's men opened fire and attacked with blades. Accounts say the reformers had pledged not to resist, and they didn't strike back.
Many were killed in the hall and the courtyard. Sikh memory holds that Bhai Lachhman Singh, wounded, was tied to the jand tree and burned. That's why pilgrims bow there.

teach.h: DO NOT STRIKE THEM IN RETURN.
teach.b: Baba Farid, whose words are in the Guru Granth Sahib at Ang 1378, says that if someone strikes you with their fists, don't strike them in return; kiss their feet and go home.
Farid is speaking of the inner life, not of a massacre. But some readers hear his salok beside Nankana, because the reformers lived it at a terrible cost.
The news spread across Punjab, and the shrine soon passed into the Panth's care.

how: Sikhs remember the Nankana massacre as the Saka Nankana Sahib, with an annual remembrance in February; pilgrims to Gurdwara Janam Asthan bow at the jand tree associated with Bhai Lachhman Singh.

games.why: accounts say they kept their pledge. many were killed, and Bhai Lachhman Singh was tied to the jand tree and burned.

practice: If you have a candle or lamp and it's safe, light it; if not, picture a small flame in front of you.

Think of people who faced violence and chose not to answer it with violence, at Nankana or anywhere, and breathe out slowly, the way you'd breathe so as not to blow the flame out. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
